refutation.quote: RL's gain on MATH-500 is mostly a reliability shift: 81% of the 198-sample gap (4 samples per problem, n=500, T 1.0, v3; base+cue 1,642 right of 2,000, RL 1,840) sits in problems the base solves at least once in 4
refutation.note: I read every item in after.jsonl and the newest 60 board items (show: result-afc423, result-429436, result-5227b9). afc423 says the MATH-500 gap sits in problems the base already solves sometimes: base 3/4 -> RL 4/4 is 43% of the gap, and only 2 problems go from 0/4 to 4/4. The base's failures on problems where one of its other samples is right are slips, misreads and format errors (39 of 48), not missing procedures. Under r4-m08, MATH-500 is the exposed set, where recall should make the base's right answers dependable. Instead the RL advantage there is about execution reliability, which is what the rival (termination and commitment) says. The scope's 'explains only part of the gap' softens this, but the scope does not exclude MATH-500 or this pair, so the result is in scope. A second piece of evidence comes from a paper the theory itself cites (Wang 2610.06851 App. C.1, via knowledge-8a31ad). On a pair close to this one (RL-Zero 3.0), the RL lead over the cued base is smaller on post-cutoff AIME 2025 (30.0 vs 22.7, 7.3 points) than on pre-cutoff AIME 2024 (35.2 vs 23.3, 11.9 points). The two sets are of similar difficulty, and the direction is the opposite of the theory's. Each set has n=30, so this is noisy. The import 2611.10307 Table 1 also reports Olmo-3-7B-Instruct with only 1.6% model-specific MATH-500 recall flags at a 60% prefix, and 0.0% for leftovers of 25 words or more. That undercuts the premise that the Olmo-3 base recalls much of MATH-500, and the GPU prediction p4 (at least 15 flagged) may fail its own count.

wins_judgement: Net gain is small (+0.12 nats): all 3 computed predictions fell inside their intervals, with no held-out claims. p1 (+0.70): the post-minus-pre gap matched on RL length came out at 6.9 points, close to the predicted 7. This is the only gain the mechanism earned. It rests on 60 post problems over 4 strata, so it is very noisy, and most of the gain comes from a tighter interval than the readers', not from a sign the readers missed: the readers' intervals contain 6.9 too. p2 (-0.80): this was the test that separates the mechanism from the rival. The theory predicted the base would be relatively shorter on pre-cutoff both-right problems (-0.3). The measured value was +0.14, the opposite sign, inside the interval only because the upper bound was 0.15. The readers (0 and -0.1) were closer. In effect the mechanism's distinctive prediction failed. p3 (+0.22): short right answers had lower per-token entropy than long ones (0.84, predicted 0.85). A reader gets the same direction without any recall: short answers are easy problems, and lower entropy on easy, correct traces is already published (2510.02611). The readers' 0.90-0.92 differ only in size, so this gain is generic. I read the script p1.py. It implements the recipe as written: join on unique_id, source label from the rln3_overlap hard flags with a source-prefix check, 4 equal strata by RL n_generated with ties broken by uid, post-weighted standardisation, and dropping strata that have post problems but no pre problems.
rival: The rival explains the numbers as well or better. p1 is consistent with the rival within noise: matching on RL length only approximates difficulty, and 60 post problems leave a wide interval. p2 is the separating test. The rival predicts no year dependence of the base/RL length ratio, the theory predicts -0.3, and the measured +0.14 sits with the rival (slightly the other way). p3 is predicted by difficulty alone. afc423 (MATH-500 gap = reliability on problems the base can solve, with slips) and 6de887/c57b51 (loops, cap hits and answer statement) also favour the rival. Still separating: p4 (gap on verbatim-completed problems vs others, not run), and a held-out split AIME 2024 vs AIME 2025 at equal difficulty on the 3.1 pair. Wang's 3.0 numbers already point against the theory there.

novelty.nearest: Yue/Wen et al. 2506.14245: the RLVR vs base CoT-Pass@K gap 'is particularly pronounced on AIME 2025, possibly due to its complete absence of unintentional data contamination, as it was released after the base model's training cutoff'. Also 2509.21882 and 2507.10532: base partial-prompt recall is high on MATH-500 and older contests but near zero on AIME 2025, and RL vs base gaps change under contamination controls.
novelty.difference: The paper attributes a larger post-cutoff RL gap to contamination in passing (Qwen2.5-32B vs DAPO, pass@k). The theory makes it a length-matched, quantitative prediction for the cued Olmo-3 base vs RL-Zero-Math 3.1, with a short, low-entropy recall signature and a verbatim-completion split.

import_carries_gain.which: Neither import carries a winning claim. 2611.10307 only feeds p4, which was not computed, and its own Table 1 (Olmo-3 has little specific MATH-500 recall) weakens the premise. 2504.13837 (RLVR concentrates on paths the base already samples) motivates the theory but sets no number in p1-p3. The one real gain, p1, comes from the year split and the length matching the theory chose itself.

verdict: weak: it survives formally, but its only gain (p1) is a noisy 60-problem estimate the readers also bracketed, its distinctive test (p2) came out with the opposite sign at the edge of the interval, p3 is a generic difficulty effect, and board result-afc423 plus the theory's own sources (Wang AIME 2024 vs 2025; Olmo-3's low recall flags in 2611.10307) favour the termination/difficulty rival.
